title: Economies of scale

blocks.heading: Economies of scale
blocks.text: Economies of scale are reductions in average cost associated with operating at a larger scale, where the relevant efficiencies are achieved. Spreading a fixed resource cost over more units or obtaining a genuine bulk-input discount can reduce cost per unit, provided the extra output is useful and manageable. Average cost means total cost divided by output. A rise in total cost does not rule out a fall in average cost. Conversely, producing more is not itself proof of an economy of scale: costs per unit may stay the same or rise. Coordination problems and unused output can undermine expected gains.

blocks.heading: Average cost with a worked example
blocks.text: A fictional group pays N$600 each month for a shared workroom. At 100 units, the room cost is N$6 per unit; at 200 units it is N$3 per unit. If other costs per unit do not rise, spreading this fixed cost helps lower average total cost. A genuine bulk-input discount can be another source. Expansion should serve demand and remain manageable; producing unsold units solely to divide the room cost by a larger number does not establish a useful development gain.
